title: AI Needs Public Feedback at Scale Before It’s Too Late | NOEMA
gist: Noema's editor argues, drawing on Hélène Landemore's essay, that OpenAI, Google and Meta's chatbots now have simultaneous two-way reach into a billion-plus people each — an unprecedented deliberative infrastructure that should be used for large-scale public input on AI governance via a three-tier framework, with direct challenges to Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg to fund it at scale.

themes.theme: Historical Pattern: Disruptive Communication Tech Eventually Self-Corrects

insights.claim: Macario Schettino's argument, cited approvingly in the piece, holds that each previous communication-driven disruption — the printing press, mass newspapers, TV and radio — was eventually tamed by the same technology that caused it, and the same pattern is expected to hold for AI-linked social media.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Sets the interpretive frame for treating current AI-driven social media chaos as a transitional phase rather than a permanent state, which matters for how investors and policymakers time expectations for AI governance stabilizing.
insights.locator: Writing in Noema, Macario Schettino has pointed out

insights.claim: Historical communication transitions took generations to stabilize: the Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia, and the mass media transition produced two world wars and a Cold War before the postwar order stabilized — implying the AI-driven social media transition, still in its early chaotic phase, could take a similarly long time to resolve.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Warns against expecting AI governance chaos to resolve quickly, a relevant baseline for long-horizon regulatory and geopolitical risk assessment around AI.
insights.quote: The Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia. The Enlightenment needed longer
insights.locator: The Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia

themes.theme: Unprecedented Scale of AI Platform Reach

insights.claim: As of mid-2026, OpenAI's ChatGPT had 900 million weekly active users in February and crossed a billion monthly users by June, while Google's Gemini grew from 400 million to over 900 million monthly active users on a similar timeline.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale at which a handful of private companies now hold direct, standing contact with global population segments larger than most nations, a structural fact relevant to AI governance and platform-risk analysis.
insights.quote: OpenAI reported 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users in February and crossed a billion monthly users in June. Google went from 400 million to more than 900 million monthly active Gemini users on a similar timeline.
insights.locator: As Hélène Landemore writes in Noema

insights.claim: Meta AI also reported a billion monthly users, meaning no government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing, two-way contact with such a huge portion of humanity simultaneously as these three AI platforms now do.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames three private companies' chatbot user bases as a novel form of global reach with no historical governmental precedent, a key input for debates on AI platform accountability and regulation.
insights.quote: No government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing, two-way contact with such a huge portion of humanity simultaneously.
insights.locator: Meta AI reported a billion monthly users as well

themes.theme: The Case for Company-Led Global AI Deliberation

insights.claim: Landemore argues that the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI right now may not be elected leaders or heads of governments, but the heads of the companies building the technology, since the infrastructure to reach hundreds of millions of people in a single week already exists via their platforms.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Reframes AI-governance legitimacy debates: private labs, not states, currently hold the practical capacity for mass deliberation, a structural argument for why regulators may be structurally behind the technology they oversee.
insights.quote: Right now, the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI may not be elected leaders and heads of governments, but the heads of the companies building this technology.
insights.locator: Right now, the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI

insights.claim: Large language models alone cannot serve as a representative proxy for humanity's interests because of the limits of their training data, meaning AI's version of reinforcement learning from human feedback needs a societal analog: broad public deliberation folded back into governance of models made by a small set of Big Tech firms.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific structural gap — training-data bias limiting models' representativeness — that argues for external public-input mechanisms rather than relying on model outputs alone as a proxy for societal values.
insights.quote: Large language models alone, despite their scope, cannot serve as representative of humanity’s interests because of the limits of their training data.
insights.locator: Large language models alone, despite their scope

themes.theme: Bias in AI Models' Values vs. Global Population

insights.claim: An Economist investigation comparing the apparent values of 25 frontier AI models to the World Values Survey across 88 countries found the models hold values more extreme than average respondents — in some cases more secular or individualist than any surveyed society on Earth — compressing the world's moral diversity.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that frontier AI models encode a narrow cultural value set rather than a global average, directly relevant to risks around AI models becoming a de facto 'global constitutional baseline' skewed toward one region's values.
insights.quote: the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent in the 88 countries surveyed by the WVS — in some cases more secular or more individualist than any society on Earth
insights.locator: Landemore notes a recent investigation by The Economist

insights.claim: Landemore's proposed first tier is an LLM-mediated global consultation that could produce an interim draft within months — a minimal, broadly endorsed statement of what a large fraction of the world wants AI to do and never do — broken out by region so it surfaces genuine divergence, such as a Western emphasis on individual data privacy versus a data-sovereignty, development-first framing common in Africa and India.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Proposes a concrete, fast, technically feasible mechanism for surfacing global AI-governance preferences, relevant to how AI companies might build legitimacy for their policy choices ahead of formal regulation.
insights.quote: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation, could produce an interim draft within months: a minimal, broadly endorsed statement of what a large fraction of the world population wants this technology to do — and never do.
insights.locator: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation

insights.claim: The second tier would be an actual real-time online global deliberation among participants, mediated by AI facilitators rather than only interacting with an AI — exemplified in practice by Engaged California, an AI-assisted public deliberation platform run by the state Office of Data and Innovation on AI's impact on work and society.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Shows a live, government-run precedent for AI-mediated mass deliberation already operating on the exact topic of AI's societal impact, a concrete model other jurisdictions or companies could replicate.
insights.quote: an actual online global deliberation, with participants interacting with each other in real time rather than only with an AI, mediated by AI facilitators.
insights.locator: The second tier would be more logistically demanding

insights.claim: The third tier would combine local and national citizens' assemblies and referenda in every country and region, feeding the results into a concluding global citizens' assembly empowered to ratify, amend, or supersede the recommendations produced by the faster first two tiers.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Provides the slowest but most legitimate layer of the proposed governance framework, designed to backstop faster AI-mediated consultation if the process has more time to unfold.
insights.quote: We could hold local and national citizens’ assemblies on key issues in every country and region, both in person and online, ideally combined with referenda where possible, then feed the results into a concluding global citizens’ assembly
insights.locator: The third tier would reach deeper still into humanity's social fabric

themes.theme: Direct Appeals to Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta

insights.claim: In 2023, Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project sourced constitutional principles from roughly 1,000 ordinary Americans and used them to tune a model, which in some areas produced less biased outputs than the standard, internally authored Anthropic model — evidence, per Landemore, that public input can improve model quality and not just confer legitimacy.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Gives investors and policymakers a documented case where crowdsourced public input measurably reduced model bias, a rare empirical link between deliberative-democracy methods and model performance.
insights.quote: In 2023, Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project sourced constitutional principles from roughly 1,000 ordinary Americans, tested and refined a real model on those principles
insights.locator: To Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

insights.claim: In 2025, Anthropic used an AI interviewer to survey nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages in a single week about how they use AI and what they hope to use it for, demonstrating that large-scale public-input methods can be executed at scale.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Establishes proof-of-concept that Anthropic already has the operational capability to run rapid, large-scale, multilingual public consultations — undercutting any claim that scale is the barrier to broader deliberation.
insights.quote: In 2025, Anthropic used an AI interviewer to ask nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages in a single week how they use AI and what they hope to use it for
insights.locator: In 2025, Anthropic used an AI interviewer

insights.claim: Despite having proven the method works, Anthropic's January 2026 'Constitution' for Claude was written the same way as its predecessor — by a small internal team, with input from the model itself and a handful of outside experts — rather than from the tens of millions of people who use the model.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Highlights a gap between Anthropic's demonstrated capability for public consultation and its actual governance practice, a governance-quality signal relevant to assessing Anthropic's stated commitments on democratic AI oversight.
insights.quote: Anthropic published a new “Constitution” for Claude, written the same way its old one was: by a small internal team, with input from the model itself and a handful of outside experts
insights.locator: What's missing isn't proof of concept

insights.claim: Tino Cuéllar, Anthropic's new chief global affairs officer and a former California Supreme Court justice who helped design Engaged California, has stated that 'democracies must set the terms on which this technology advances' — a public commitment Landemore's essay directly challenges Anthropic to act on.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Names a specific Anthropic executive and stated policy position that can be tracked against future company actions on public AI governance input.
insights.quote: democracies must set the terms on which this technology advances
insights.locator: It is a good sign that Tino Cuéllar

insights.claim: OpenAI's 2023 'Democratic Inputs to AI' program funded 10 teams selected from nearly 1,000 applicants to prototype public-input methods, but per Landemore, a former advisor to the program, it never scaled to match OpenAI's actual user reach.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Documents an underdelivered OpenAI initiative on public AI governance input, relevant to assessing the credibility gap between OpenAI's stated democratic-input ambitions and its execution at scale.
insights.quote: This never amounted to anything close to what OpenAI’s reach could support.
insights.locator: To Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI

insights.claim: Meta ran a 2022 Community Forum on Cyberbullying in the Metaverse with Stanford's Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioral Insights Team, gathering input from small-group online deliberations among nearly 6,500 people across 32 countries, followed by two further 2023-2024 Community Forums on generative AI issues with 1,000+ participants each.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Shows Meta already has a working, tested model for large-scale AI-related public deliberation, making Landemore's call to scale it to Meta AI's billion-person reach a request to extend an existing capability rather than build a new one.
insights.quote: It gathered input from small-group online deliberations among nearly 6,500 people across 32 countries in 2022 on the issue of harassment occurring within your virtual reality platform.
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

insights.claim: Landemore calls on Meta to relaunch its Community Forums on AI at billion-person scale — not as one-off sentiment-measuring pilots, but as a standing global institution that democracies have never had the tools to build.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Sets a specific, trackable benchmark — a standing global deliberation institution — against which Meta's future AI governance practices can be measured.
insights.quote: not as a couple of one-off pilots measuring sentiment, but as a standing global institution that democracies have never had the tools to build.
insights.locator: it's time to redo the Community Forums on AI at that scale

insights.claim: Landemore's essay closes with an appeal to every other tech leader in the U.S., China and beyond to help fund democratically written global and local AI constitutions, arguing no government currently has the speed, will, or standing to do it alone.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames private AI companies, not states, as the necessary funders and enablers of global AI governance legitimacy in the near term — a structural claim with direct implications for how regulatory risk should be weighted against corporate self-governance initiatives.
insights.quote: Help bring democratically written global and local constitutions on AI into being, because right now no government is moving fast enough, or has the will or standing, to do it alone.
insights.locator: Landemore closes her essay with a broader appeal
